7.text: Then she enters the sleeping-room, takes off her racing-dress, unties the

8.text: boots of the young man, and helps him to take off boots and breeches. She

9.text: gives him her own racing-dress. Then she cuts off the long tassel from his

10.text: own fur shirt and pins it to her usual woman’s dress. She burns the rest of

11.text: his clothes in the fire. Then she says to her father, “This night I shall not

12.text: go to the herd.” — “All right!” says the father. She cooks some supper

13.text: and carries it into the sleeping-room. After supper she prepares their bed in

14.text: the corner of the sleeping-room. She spreads some soft skins, lays out the

15.text: pillow, and brings a blanket of new skins. Then she helps him to take off

16.text: his clothes, and says, “Lie down to sleep.” She covers him with the blanket;

19.text: In some tales of this type the parents are willing to accept the suitor,

20.text: and even help him to conquer the heart of the stubborn beauty. In other

21.text: tales the neighbors, the people living in the same camp or village, are hostile

22.text: to the suitor, and try to take his life. Several tales describe the adventures

23.text: of the suitor, who comes to an alien camp or village, and is welcomed by

24.text: the people who occupy one of the poorest houses. He marries the daughter

25.text: of his host. Then the master of the principal house,² or, in other tales, the

26.text: brothers of the bride, who live in the surrounding houses, or the whole popu-

27.text: lation of the village, say, “Let us have some fun with this bridegroom.” Then

28.text: follows a series of matches and fights, in which the new-comer usually gets

29.text: the upper hand. After that he takes his wife and returns to his own country.

30.text: In olden times, marriages with people of an alien camp or village may

31.text: have been accompanied by adventures and difficulties of this kind.

32.text: The practice of meeting a new-comer with some severe test of his courage

33.text: and physical strength is often described in Chukchee tales, even without

34.text: reference to marriage. It is arranged by the “front-house master,” and per-

35.text: formed in the “front house.” The same practice is described by several

36.text: authors as really existing among the American Eskimo. Dr. Franz Boas

37.text: (Central Eskimo, p. 609) says, “that if a stranger unknown to the inhabitants of

38.text: a settlement arrives on a visit, he is welcomed by the celebration of a great

39.text: festival. The stranger approaches slowly, his arms folded, and his head inclined

40.text: toward the right side. Then the native strikes him with all his strength on

41.text: the right cheek, and in his turn inclines the head, awaiting the stranger’s blow.
